thread.title: The Dow Sinks Because There's More to Worry About Than Oil and Apple

title: The Dow Sinks Because There's More to Worry About Than Oil and Apple
text:
The Dow Sinks Because There’s More to Worry About Than Oil and Apple By Nov. 14, 2018 11:58 a.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Michael Haddad Text size
Crunch Time . Stocks are lower Wednesday as investors balance largely positive news on inflation with ominous China data and worries about Brexit. In today’s Intraday Update, we… ...note news from around the world; ...posit what could feed a year-end rally; and ...see wildfire worries are sinking PG&E again.
Worry Wall
Stocks were moving down at midday Wednesday: The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 were off 0.2% and the Nasdaq Composite was 0.3% lower.
There were a few things causing investor concern, including uncertainty around the latest Brexit developments , the fact that Germany’s economy shrank for the first time in more than three years, and mixed data from China, which showed slowing retail sales but an uptick in industrial output and investment.
On the home front, October consumer prices rose in line with expectations. Although the 0.3% increase was the fastest rate since the beginning of the year, much of that can be attributed to gasoline prices, so the recent fall in crude may provide welcome relief.
Consumer prices are of concern to investors, given the Federal Reserve’s focus on inflation. “The price of moderate inflation is eternal vigilance. That seems to be the Fed’s strategy and it makes sense,” writes Naroff Economic Advisors’ Joel Naroff . Newsletter Sign-up
While some may argue that the central bank is fighting a war against nonexistent inflation, he argues that that’s not the case. “The Fed’s reasoning for raising rates is not that inflation is too high or the risk to inflation getting out of control is significant...the members recognize that there are forces at work, in particular, massive fiscal stimulus at a time of labor shortages, that could potentially lead to inflation accelerating. So, the logical approach is to position monetary policy so that the Fed can fight inflation if the need arises.”
But wait, there are more factors keeping investors awake at night. There’s still uncertainty about tariffs, and market-shaking headlines like softer demand for Apple ’s (AAPL) iPhones.
Yet even with all these worries, the “year-end rally thesis is stressed, but not broken,” argues Fundstrat Global Advisors’ Thomas Lee . He says that looking further out, inflation expectations are shifting, and market leadership styles are likely to change with it, with a return to value, and asset-intensive business models outperforming. Nearer term, however, he’s still confident in the market’s ability to push higher, writing “this pullback needs to be bought.”
So a Santa rally is still in the cards, but what about 2019? That doesn’t look so bad either, says UBS ’s Yianos Kontopoulos . He sees a 70% probability that the asset cycle stays in “expansion mode” next year. The underpinnings of the global cycle are still positive, and he expects high-single digit returns for developed and emerging market equities, and a rise in U.S. interest rates with a flattening curve—although both moves should be smaller than we saw this year. That said, investors should stay vigilant, as “key macro developments in 2019 imply more uncertainty and higher risks, as the global cycle matures,” Kontopoulos writes.
Maturity, or “adulting,” may not be fun, but things could be worse.
Midday Movers
Apple (AAPL) was down 1.8% to $188.98 after Guggenheim downgraded it to Neutral.
Carlyle Group (CG) was down 0.5% to $18.97. Morgan Stanley downgraded it to Equal Weight.
Conagra (CAG) fell 6.5% to $32.91 after Bernstein downgraded it to Underperform.
O’Reilly Automotive (ORL) rose 1% to $361.09 after adding $1 billion to its stock repurchase plan and saying it will acquire Florida-based Bennett Auto Supply, which operates 33 stores.
PG&E (PCG) was down 18.9% to $26.54. The California utility warned in a regulator filing it could be subject to “significant” liability in excess of its insurance coverage.
